description: Cross-cutting failure patterns. Learning chains reference them by id in 'failure_patterns'. Every pattern carries 'evidence_kind' from vocabularies.evidence_kinds; a mined pattern becomes observed when an agent reproduces it in Revit.

patterns.name: Geometry correct, semantics wrong
patterns.meaning: The shape is right but the category, role or family kind is wrong for downstream use.

patterns.name: Wrong coordinate frame or orientation
patterns.meaning: Mirrored views, wrong view direction, assumed camera, transforms defaulting to world axes.

patterns.name: Existing content should have been reused
patterns.meaning: A governed family, parameter or standard existed and was recreated.

patterns.name: Missing fabrication or material constraint
patterns.meaning: The layout is geometrically valid but cannot be built from stock material.

patterns.name: API succeeded, model result wrong
patterns.meaning: The call returned without error but Revit changed something else (auto-joins, ignored defaults, silent overrides). Defence: after placement or modification at scale, verify positions after commit and regeneration, not at call time.

evidence.note: Document.AutoJoinElements discussion: when a transaction is committed, Revit automatically joins elements to their neighbours where appropriate, so geometry verified at placement time can silently change at commit. This is the documented mechanism behind the framing-stud case in ARPL-ASM-0004.

patterns.name: Correct model, unusable schedule or data
patterns.meaning: Values exist but can't be scheduled, totalled or extracted.

patterns.name: Correct element, wrong authority
patterns.meaning: A value or decision was taken by the agent that belongs to the user, a standard or a discipline.

patterns.name: Correct geometry, documentation fails
patterns.meaning: Views, crops, dimensions or sheets don't show the model correctly.

patterns.name: Source misread
patterns.meaning: A dimension, view or note in the source document was missed or misinterpreted.

patterns.name: Dependency not propagated
patterns.meaning: A change in one element left dependents (profile walls, levels, hosted inserts, sheets) unchanged.

patterns.name: Runtime blocked by a dialog
patterns.meaning: A modal Revit dialog or warning blocked the automation; nothing visible in the API result. Defence: unattended bridges must register a failure preprocessor (IFailuresPreprocessor) and a DialogBoxShowing handler before the first batch write, or a single warning freezes the run.

evidence.note: Two documented suppression routes: the DialogBoxShowing event (dismiss a dialog programmatically) and the Revit 2011 failure processing API, which does more than dialog suppression. An unattended run without one of these blocks silently.

patterns.name: Fix incomplete
patterns.meaning: The correction addressed one case of the problem; the same problem reappeared in a neighbouring case.

patterns.name: Frame chosen from a name
patterns.meaning: The agent picks the domain, discipline or meaning of a task from a familiar word (a name, an acronym, 'connector', 'panel', 'room', 'system') before inspecting the actual evidence, then executes valid operations in the wrong world. Rule: Identify -> Inspect -> Frame -> Act, not Recognize -> Assume -> Act.
patterns.example: Given the link github.com/gschmidtke/ARPL, an AI described 'ARPL (Advanced Redpill Loader)', an unrelated NAS bootloader, without opening the repository, and even attributed that project to the wrong owner. Revit equivalent: 'create the equipment connector' read as electrical when the family is audio equipment.
patterns.found_by: user noticed the answer did not match the source

patterns.name: Exception leaves a transaction open
patterns.meaning: A scripted error escapes while the script's own Transaction is still open. Inside an enclosing TransactionGroup this can crash Revit (fatal error) instead of failing the script. Defence: using-blocks for every Transaction, try/catch around the body, dry runs. See FP28: the using-block pattern is the defence, and also the trap when Commit is never reached.
patterns.found_by: Revit journal after a fatal error

evidence.note: Arnost Lobel's transaction advice series: scope transactions in using-blocks (which automagically dispose and roll back), check transaction status, and handle transaction groups deliberately - the foundation of the FP14 defence.

patterns.name: Shared assembly type edited through one instance
patterns.meaning: Adding or removing members of an AssemblyInstance whose AssemblyType is used by other instances makes Revit ask (modal dialog, not a failure message) whether to update the type. The failures preprocessor cannot answer it, the API call blocks until a person does, and the change may be copied to every instance (members duplicated over the other instances). Defence: before editing members, count instances of the type; if more than one, create a new assembly from the new members instead and delete the old instance with its members.
patterns.found_by: Bridge timeout; owner at the Revit dialog

patterns.name: New assembly frame follows the project axes
patterns.meaning: AssemblyInstance.Create gives the assembly a transform along the project X/Y axes, not along the element it describes. Assembly views (CreateDetailSection elevations, plan sections) and any dimensions computed in the assembly frame then look at the wrong side or collapse to one segment. Defence: after creating an assembly for a wall panel, call SetTransform so BasisX runs along the wall and BasisY points to the interior, before creating its views.
patterns.found_by: West shop drawing came out with one stud dimension

patterns.name: Modal warning raised inside an API call
patterns.meaning: Some Revit API calls post a warning as a modal dialog during the call itself, before the script can change the condition (ElectricalSystem.Create checks the load against the default 20 A rating). The transaction's failures preprocessor does not see it; the bridge call blocks until a person answers. Defence: anticipate the condition (temporary small load, set limits first), and when a bridge call times out, look at the screen before anything else.
patterns.found_by: Bridge timeout, screenshot

patterns.name: Stale geometry references after regeneration
patterns.meaning: Face references collected before other elements were placed on the same host can be invalid after a regeneration; using them for face-based placement throws a native SEHException instead of a managed error. Defence: fetch the host's face references immediately before each placement.
patterns.found_by: SEHException that did not reproduce in an isolated test

patterns.name: Unknown tool parameter silently ignored
patterns.meaning: A misspelled or unsupported parameter (here mode instead of transaction) is dropped without an error, so the call runs with defaults: scripts that start their own Transaction fail inside the default wrapper. Defence: load the tool schema before the first call and check the reported transaction mode in the result.
patterns.found_by: "Starting a new transaction is not permitted" from a script that had worked before

patterns.name: Application reminder dialog blocks an automated run
patterns.meaning: Revit's periodic "Changes Not Synchronized with Central" reminder is modal and stops a running command past the bridge timeout; a partial run can leave half-finished state (old views deleted, new ones not yet created). Defence: screenshot on every timeout, dismiss the reminder, read the model state before re-running.
patterns.found_by: screenshot after a 60 s timeout

patterns.name: Read-only collection returned by the API
patterns.meaning: ViewSheetSet.Views is a read-only ViewSet; Insert throws and, inside a TransactionGroup, rolls back everything before it. Defence: build a new ViewSet and assign it through PrintManager.ViewSheetSetting, and keep optional steps in their own try block.
patterns.found_by: InvalidOperationException "Collection is read-only"

patterns.name: Long export outlives the call timeout
patterns.meaning: A combined PDF export of 14+ sheets takes over 60 s; the bridge call times out while Revit keeps exporting. Defence: watch the status bar until it reads Ready, then check the file size and time before the next command.
patterns.found_by: status bar progress in a screenshot

evidence.note: Not only exports: a single run_csharp write call creating levels, slabs, columns and walls outlived the 60 s bridge timeout, and a read-only follow-up timed out too, while Revit had committed everything. Re-running would have duplicated every element. Defence: keep each write stage well inside the timeout, never retry a write after a timeout, and query the model by Mark before deciding (ARPL-GEO-0004).

Cloud operations too: SaveAsCloudModel plus EnableCloudWorksharing took 60-90 s and outlived the bridge reply every time; during 'Enable Worksharing' further calls also timed out. The model was uploaded each time. Defence: one long call per model, then wait and read IsModelInCloud / IsWorkshared / the cloud model GUID in a short call; never resend (ARPL-ADM-0003).

patterns.name: Viewport outline inflated by elements outside the crop
patterns.meaning: Section marks, camera markers and similar elements beyond the crop region set the viewport outline, so a rescaled view looks too big for its sheet; an automatic packer then moves it away. Defence: crop and annotation-crop first, find elements whose view bounding box extends past the crop, trim or hide them, and never empty a single-view sheet.
patterns.found_by: sheet fit check plus an element search against the crop box

patterns.name: Local cloud cache exhausts the disk during a batch run
patterns.meaning: Every cloud model opened or synced is copied into the local collaboration cache (CollaborationCache under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Autodesk\Revit\<version>). A batch over many models can fill the drive mid-run; Revit then fails saves or syncs in ways that look like model or network errors. Defence: check free space before a batch (several GB per dozen models), and let the user clear the cache with Revit closed; never delete it from a running session.
patterns.found_by: user noticed under 100 MB free after an aborted batch relinking run

patterns.name: Dependency inferred from a message string
patterns.meaning: A help text, dialog message or log line names features that need a credential, licence or service, and the agent repeats it as fact. Such strings are often older than the code. Defence: confirm a dependency from the behaviour (does the command run without it?) or from the code path, and name the source when reporting it.
patterns.found_by: the tool's author corrected the claim; the code path confirmed one command, not several

patterns.name: Internal database units assumed
patterns.meaning: The Revit API returns and expects raw database units; length is feet and area is square feet, regardless of the project's display units. A '200 mm' wall reads as 0.656 in the API. An agent that writes millimetre or metre values into geometry calls produces a model wrong by a factor of 304.8 or 3.28 - with no error, no warning, no failed call. Defence: Treat every raw API length as feet and every area as square feet. Never mix project display units into geometry calls. Convert explicitly (UnitUtils, or the 0.3048 factor) only at display and export boundaries. Sanity-check one known dimension against the UI before any batch write.
patterns.found_by: mined from The Building Coder archive
patterns.revit_versions: all; conversion API changed in 2021 (UnitTypeId), the underlying database units did not

patterns.name: Stale geometry read after modify
patterns.meaning: After changing an element (parameter, location, type), geometry queried before regeneration or commit reflects the old state. In batch workflows and manual regeneration mode this becomes systematic: the agent measures and validates against yesterday's model. Source quote: 'The only problem is the risk of missing a regeneration and retrieving stale data.' Defence: Modify, then regenerate (or commit), then measure. Never read geometry to validate a change made in the same unregenerated pass. Regenerating more often than necessary is cheap; a stale read is invisible. After any write through a bridge, force a refresh (RefreshActiveView / UpdateAllOpenViews where available) before any verification pass, in addition to regenerate-then-read.
patterns.found_by: mined from The Building Coder archive
patterns.revit_versions: regeneration modes changed in 2011; the stale-read trap persists in batch code

evidence.note: A pyRevit-based bridge's own tracker documents that views do not repaint after tool calls (element creation, colour overrides in inactive views) until the user clicks or pans, so 'users think the tool didn't work'. The same stale-state trap hits agents that verify visually or by re-reading before a refresh.

patterns.related: FP18 (sibling: FP18 is face references invalidated by regeneration, FP27 is geometry read before regeneration)

patterns.name: Uncommitted transaction rolls back silently
patterns.meaning: A Transaction in a using-block that never reaches Commit() disposes and rolls back with no exception: the code appears to succeed and the model is unchanged. The opposite face (an exception escaping with an open transaction crashing Revit inside a TransactionGroup) is already FP14; this entry adds the silent-rollback side, which is the one an agent cannot notice from the return values alone. Defence: Commit explicitly inside the using block, check the returned TransactionStatus, and treat RollBack-on-dispose as a failure path, not a default. Wrap the body in try/catch so no exception escapes with the transaction open. After any batch: read back a sample of changes to confirm they exist. For agent workflows spanning multiple tool calls, request a TransactionGroup wrapper so the run is atomic and undoable as one unit; keep read-back verification after every batch regardless.
patterns.found_by: mined from The Building Coder archive
patterns.revit_versions: all

evidence.note: Two additions: a feature request to wrap an entire multi-call AI task in one TransactionGroup so a whole agent run is undoable in a single step (the community independently re-deriving FP33's mechanism for agent workflows); and the concurrency issue recorded as FP35 showing four model edits skipped while their callers received success — read-back verification is the only defence that catches both.

patterns.name: API call outside valid Revit context
patterns.meaning: Revit API calls are valid only inside an API context (external command, ExternalEvent). Called from background threads, timers or modeless dialogs they fail unpredictably: a transaction 'refuses to start for no apparent reason', a call that worked before fails 'except for the exact time', sometimes Revit records errors only in the journal or crashes. Intermittent, non-reproducible failures are the signature. Defence: Never call the Revit API from a thread or UI callback. Marshal every request through a raised ExternalEvent and keep Idling as a last resort. If an API call fails intermittently with no code change, suspect the calling context before the call. Treat a timeout as 'state unknown', not 'call failed': never blindly re-issue an identical write (double-apply risk); check for a blocking dialog, a busy Revit, or a dead ExternalEvent first, and make write retries idempotent.
patterns.found_by: mined from The Building Coder archive
patterns.revit_versions: all; the canonical explanation is Arnost Lobel's (Revit development team)

evidence.note: A timeout is often the only symptom of a context failure: on one bridge, the TCP connection establishes but Revit never responds, and every command, including trivial ones, times out after 30 seconds. The agent gets no context error — just silence — and a write that timed out client-side may still execute inside Revit later.

patterns.related: FP20, FP22 (a timeout means state unknown: read the screen and the model before re-running)

patterns.name: Modification attempted in read-only context
patterns.meaning: Many event handlers (DocumentChanged, ViewActivated, application-level events) are notification-only: the document cannot be modified inside the handler. An agent that 'reacts to an event' with direct edits gets an exception or a silent no-op, and the event list is shorter than agents assume. Defence: Event handlers only record and queue. Every model edit goes through an ExternalEvent raised from the handler and executed later in a valid, writable context.
patterns.found_by: mined from The Building Coder archive
patterns.revit_versions: all

patterns.name: Name-based parameter lookup ambiguity
patterns.meaning: Name-based parameter lookups return the first match and null on no match. With shared and project parameter name collisions, or family versus type parameters, an agent silently reads or writes the wrong parameter, or dereferences null and the run dies mid-batch. Defence: Prefer BuiltInParameter or parameter GUID lookups. Null-check every parameter before use. When only a name is available, verify the result (owning element, definition, storage type) before reading or writing. Treat a duplicate name as an error, not a first-match windfall.
patterns.found_by: mined from The Building Coder archive
patterns.revit_versions: all

patterns.name: Posted command assumed immediate
patterns.meaning: PostCommand queues a built-in command for the idle state; it does not execute inline. Code that posts a command and then reads or edits the model runs before the command executes, so results are stale or the context is invalid. Defence: Treat a posted command as fire-and-forget: schedule any follow-up work in an ExternalEvent, and never read model state in the same call sequence assuming the posted command already ran.
patterns.found_by: mined from The Building Coder archive
patterns.revit_versions: 2014+; custom-command posting needed UR1 to work consistently

evidence.note: Reproduced by an agent in Revit 2024: an add-in command posted through the bridge did not start until the mouse moved over the Revit window; its file picker, the OS overwrite prompt and its result dialog then blocked the bridge (calls timed out) until closed. Defence: after posting, move the mouse over the application, screenshot, handle each dialog, and only then send the next bridge call (ARPL-ADM-0003).

patterns.name: Dry-run transaction group assimilated instead of rolled back
patterns.meaning: TransactionGroup.Assimilate() merges the enclosed sub-transactions into one committed change; RollBack() undoes them. An agent that wraps a dry run in a TransactionGroup and calls Assimilate on the 'success' path commits exactly the changes it meant to discard - no error, full undo history pointing at the agent. Defence: Dry run always ends in TransactionGroup.RollBack(). Call Assimilate only after validation passed. After the group ends, read back a sample before the next step to confirm the document is in the expected state.
patterns.found_by: mined from The Building Coder archive
patterns.related: FP28 (family: silent success that is not success)

patterns.name: Advertised tool contract desync
patterns.meaning: The bridge's advertised contract and its actual behaviour disagree, in two documented faces. (a) Registry desync: tools/list advertises tools the Revit side never registered. Agents call them and get 'Method not found' while every genuinely registered tool works; root-caused in the archived revit-mcp as implemented C# commands missing from the plugin's command manifest, so they were implemented but undiscoverable. An agent in this state burned multiple turns rotating through ai_element_filter, get_current_view_elements, send_code_to_revit and get_available_family_types, all listed, all 'not found', on two machines and two Revit versions. (b) Schema desync: a tool's JSON schema advertises null as the default for optional arguments, but the validator rejects null when a client actually sends it. Agent frameworks that fill every optional field from the schema get validation errors on tools that would have run had the field been omitted. Defence: Treat tools/list and tool schemas as unverified advertisement, not ground truth. On 'Method not found' or an argument-validation error on an advertised tool, do not rewrite the request: probe a known-good cheap tool to separate channel faults from contract faults, then degrade to the tools that verifiably respond, and report the desync instead of iterating. When composing parallel plans, fill only arguments with real values and omit optionals rather than sending advertised defaults.
patterns.found_by: mined from Revit MCP-server issue trackers
patterns.revit_versions: Revit 2020-2026; client- and bridge-agnostic (reported on Claude Desktop and direct JSON-RPC)
patterns.related: FP19 (sibling: FP19 is an unknown parameter silently ignored by the tool, FP34 is the advertised contract itself being wrong)

patterns.name: Parallel tool calls share one handler (false success, wrong data)
patterns.meaning: Bridges built on a single module-level request handler / ExternalEvent cannot serve concurrent requests. When an MCP client (which issues tool calls in parallel by default) sends overlapping API-context calls, only some handlers execute, and every waiting caller receives the same response, all with HTTP 200. Model edits are skipped while their callers are told they succeeded, and follow-up requests are answered with the previous request's response until the server idles. No exception, no log entry: in the documented repro, six concurrent calls each received one handler's answer, only two of six handlers ran, and four model edits were skipped while reported as successful. Root-caused upstream in pyRevit Routes (one shared handler per request thread), fixed upstream, but the agent-facing fault class generalises to any single-threaded host bridge. Defence: Never issue concurrent API-context tool calls; serialise all tool traffic to one Revit session. Treat HTTP 200 as unproven: after any write, read back the changed state before declaring success. If a bridge is known to serialise internally, still verify writes, because residual races remain (two server processes on one Revit, or a client-side timeout while the call still executes inside Revit, which re-applies on retry).
patterns.found_by: mined from Revit MCP-server issue trackers
patterns.revit_versions: pyRevit 6.x/7.0 era; generalises to any bridge that funnels requests through one handler on a single-threaded host
patterns.related: FP28 (family: silent success that is not success)

patterns.name: Bridge rejects or drops a valid request (channel faults that blame the caller)
patterns.meaning: Transport- and protocol-level faults surface as errors that accuse the agent's request. A well-formed JSON-RPC body is answered with 'Invalid JSON' (-32700) because the plugin's embedded HTTP server omits the HTTP status line, so the response parses as HTTP/0.9. Node.js resolves 'localhost' to IPv6 ::1 while the Revit plugin listens on IPv4 only, so every tool call fails with ECONNREFUSED although the server is up and the requests are perfect. The agent's natural response — rewriting the payload, alternating encodings, retrying with variations — cannot succeed, and the transcript shows the agent unable to distinguish its own malformed request from a broken channel. Defence: On a transport or parse error, verify the channel before touching the payload: connect by explicit 127.0.0.1 rather than localhost, probe the port, call a known-good healthcheck tool. Never 'fix' a request that was well-formed; distinguish 'request invalid' from 'channel broken' before any retry; cap the retry loop and escalate rather than mutate.
patterns.found_by: mined from Revit MCP-server issue trackers
patterns.revit_versions: reported on Revit 2024-2025, Windows 10/11, Node 17+; the IPv6/IPv4 and HTTP/0.9 mechanisms are version-independent

patterns.name: Name mangling across the serialization boundary
patterns.meaning: Non-ASCII element names (Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic, umlauts, accents) are replaced with '?' by ASCII-fallback normalization on the bridge side. Listing tools return names like '????? 1'; the agent then sends the mangled name back into any lookup-by-name tool, and the lookup fails. The agent reads this as 'element not found' and iterates on the lookup, when the element exists and its name was destroyed in transit. Documented on a pyRevit/IronPython bridge where str vs unicode matters, with an independent fix in a community fork confirming the fault recurs across implementations. This is the string face of the class FP26 covers for numbers: values corrupted crossing the bridge boundary, invisibly, with the round-trip as the trap. Defence: Prefer ElementId over names as the round-trip key across any bridge. On first listing, test name integrity: fetch a name, query by it, and treat clusters of '?' or mojibake as a corruption signal, not as data. When a lookup fails for a name just returned by a listing tool, suspect boundary corruption before concluding the element is absent.
patterns.found_by: mined from Revit MCP-server issue trackers
patterns.revit_versions: pyRevit/IronPython 2.7 era bridges; the ASCII-fallback mechanism is bridge- and version-independent
patterns.related: FP26 (sibling: boundary corrupts the value; FP26 corrupts numbers by unit convention, this corrupts strings by encoding)

patterns.name: Generated code compiled inside the host inherits an invisible environment
patterns.meaning: Agent-authored C# sent to a code-execution tool is compiled by the bridge inside Revit, against an environment the agent cannot see. Three documented failure faces, one class: (a) the compiler adds every assembly loaded in the AppDomain as a metadata reference, so a third-party add-in with protected DLLs makes compilation fail before the agent's code is even parsed; (b) the bridge ships Roslyn with newer dependencies than the Revit release bundles, throwing a type-initializer exception on one Revit version while the identical call succeeds on the adjacent version; (c) Revit 2026 moved to .NET 8, which removed CodeDom compilation, so the legacy CSharpCodeProvider path throws 'Operation is not supported on this platform' — on Revit 2022 the same code ran. In all three faces the agent's code was correct, the compilation environment failed, and the transcripts show agents iterating on their own code, then falling back to manual instructions. Defence: After a compile failure of generated code, first compile a minimal known-good template. If the template fails, the environment is at fault: stop, report an environmental failure, and do not rewrite working code. Pin the compile target to the host's runtime (.NET Framework 4.8 vs .NET 8), expect platform shifts between Revit releases, and treat 'works on one release, fails on the neighbour' as an environment signature.
patterns.found_by: mined from Revit MCP-server issue trackers
patterns.revit_versions: Revit 2021-2026; the .NET Framework 4.8 to .NET 8 shift lands in 2026

patterns.name: Assumed execution-context variables in generated code
patterns.meaning: Code-execution bridges inject the Revit context through template variables whose names are an unstated contract. The archived revit-mcp template exposed only lowercase 'document', while agents write 'Document' or 'doc' following the Dynamo and macro conventions, and expect 'uidoc' for selection work. The agent's code fails to access the current document although the document is passed to the executor, and the failure reads to the agent as a Revit API problem, or as its own hallucination — the reporter's own framing was 'wondering if this is a hallucination or fact?'. The fix was bridge-side aliases, confirming the contract, not the API, was at fault. The agent's own stack-trace diagnosis confidently blamed the wrong layer. Defence: Before writing real code against a code-execution tool, probe the execution contract: run a trivial template that returns the available context variables and their types. Never assume Dynamo or macro naming. On a 'variable not found' or 'cannot access document' error, print the available scope first and treat the template contract as the suspect, not the Revit API.
patterns.found_by: mined from Revit MCP-server issue trackers
patterns.revit_versions: documented on the archived revit-mcp bridge; the class applies to any generated-code tool with an injected scope
patterns.related: FP38 (sibling: generated code fails on an invisible contract; FP38 is the compile environment, FP39 is the runtime scope)

patterns.name: API member assumed from another Revit version
patterns.meaning: Generated code calls API members the agent remembers from another Revit release or from documentation, not from the installed API. In a Revit 2024 build, Wall.AddAttachment and AttachmentLocation did not exist, NonContinuousRailInfo had no public constructor, and a bridge helper name was guessed; each cost a compile round. Unlike FP38 the compile environment was fine: the agent's code was wrong. Defence: before using non-trivial members (wall attachment, rails, stairs, failure handling), reflect the installed types (GetMethods, GetConstructors) or compile a probe, and write against what exists. Revit 2024 equivalents found: profile walls instead of attachment (ARPL-GEO-0002); RailingType.RailStructure.AddNonContinuousRail(name, height, offset), then configure ProfileId; StairsEditScope.Commit with an IFailuresPreprocessor.
patterns.found_by: Roslyn compile errors, resolved by reflecting the installed types
patterns.revit_versions: observed in 2024; members differ between releases
patterns.related: FP38 (sibling: FP38 is the compile environment failing correct code; FP40 is the code itself written against a remembered API), FP34 (the bridge's advertised contract)

evidence.note: TessellatedShapeBuilderResult.GetNumberOfIssues was assumed and does not exist in Revit 2024; a compile round lost (ARPL-GEO-0005).

patterns.name: Desktop action reaches the wrong window or instance
patterns.meaning: Desktop-control actions act on whatever the operating system gives them, not on the model the agent means. Opening an application that is already running can start a second, empty instance instead of focusing the running one; typed text goes to whichever window has focus, for example the chat window that came to the front. Defence: never use open-application on a running Revit; prefer API routes (Document.ExportImage of a dedicated view) for visual checks; before typing into a dialog, click into its input field and confirm with a screenshot or zoom.
patterns.found_by: screenshot showing a second Revit splash; bridge status listing two live sessions; a screenshot with the chat window in front of a file dialog
patterns.revit_versions: observed in 2024; desktop layer, not the Revit API

patterns.name: Null-conditional parameter write skips silently
patterns.meaning: get_Parameter(...)?.Set(...) does nothing when the element has no such parameter, and the null-conditional hides it. 261 grids were 'tagged' with Comments, but grid datums have no ALL_MODEL_INSTANCE_COMMENTS, so no tag was written and a read-back found 0 grids. Defence: where a tag or value matters, fetch the parameter, fail loudly when it is null or read-only, and identify datums by a unique name prefix instead.
patterns.found_by: read-back by tag returned 0 of 261
patterns.revit_versions: observed in 2024
patterns.related: FP05 (API succeeded, model result wrong), FP31 (name-based parameter lookup)

patterns.name: Template placeholder taken as a real value
patterns.meaning: Project templates ship with placeholder text in Project Information ('Building Name', 'Project Name'). The value is not empty, so tools that ask only for a missing value take the placeholder as real data: a model registry got 'Building Name' as a model key. Defence: before any step that reads identity fields, set them explicitly, and treat known placeholder strings as missing.
patterns.found_by: reading the registry CSV
patterns.revit_versions: any; template content

patterns.name: Nearest-distance assignment misfiles elements
patterns.meaning: Assigning elements to a building (or zone) by the nearest bounding box fails where buildings touch: a floor centre can be closer to the neighbour's box than to its own, so one building loses elements and its neighbour gains them. Defence: assign by containment in the owner's own extent (smallest containing extent wins), and check that per-group counts add up to the source total with nothing unassigned.
patterns.found_by: per-file counts: one building with 0 floors, its neighbour with too many
patterns.revit_versions: any; algorithmic

patterns.name: Document state read from the path string
patterns.meaning: After a failed or late-failing SaveAsCloudModel (name already exists), Document.PathName showed the cloud path although nothing had been saved: IsModelInCloud false, IsModified true, and EnableCloudWorksharing failed with 'does not have a central location'. An agent that judges success by PathName or by the title bar is wrong. Defence: read IsModelInCloud, IsWorkshared and GetCloudModelPath() (which throws for a non-cloud document).
patterns.found_by: GetCloudModelPath threw 'not a cloud model' while PathName showed the cloud path
patterns.revit_versions: observed in 2024
patterns.related: FP22 (the exception arrived after the reply timeout)

patterns.name: Generated default contradicts the project setup
patterns.meaning: A tool-generated configuration (here a host-by-link matrix exported from a registry) carries defaults that contradict decisions already made for the project: 'use shared coordinates' was false on every row of a federation built on shared coordinates. Run as generated, every link would have been placed origin to origin. Defence: before a batch run, read the generated configuration against the project's setup (coordinates, worksets, load behaviour) and change it on a backup copy.
patterns.found_by: reading the matrix values before the run
patterns.revit_versions: any; tool configuration

patterns.name: Planned penetrations counted as clashes
patterns.meaning: A geometric clash run reports every crossing, including services that are meant to pass through an element (a pipe dropping through a ceiling to a fixture, a duct through a wall with an opening still to come). Counted as clashes they bury the real conflicts and make the number meaningless. Defence: classify before reporting (direction of the run, modelled opening, category rule) and report penetrations separately; check fittings at those points by hand until they can be classified.
patterns.found_by: reading the clash list by orientation of the running element
patterns.revit_versions: any

patterns.name: Expected cloud service missing from the project
patterns.meaning: A workflow was planned around a cloud service (clash detection in ACC Model Coordination) that the project's subscription does not include; the project menu showed Data Management, Build, Design and admin modules only, and the product had been renamed (Autodesk Forma), so the expected entry was not where the instructions said. Defence: before planning on a cloud service, open the project's module list and confirm it; keep a bridge-based fallback (ARPL-CRD-0001).
patterns.found_by: user screenshots of the project module menu
patterns.revit_versions: any; cloud platform

patterns.name: Completeness scored against an assumed requirement
patterns.meaning: A fill-rate score is reported before the client's information requirement exists, with every schedule column assumed required. The number looks precise but measures the assumption: one optional field (Description) halved the score. Defence: print the assumption next to the number, and replace it with the client's LOIN table per category and stage as soon as it exists.
patterns.found_by: comparing the score with what the client actually asked for
patterns.revit_versions: any

patterns.name: Batch report describes links as the batch opened them
patterns.meaning: A batch tool opens each model with link worksets closed for speed; its health and placement reports then show every link as unloaded or in a closed workset, placement 'not checked', and instance names without the shared site. Read as project state, these would be false findings. Defence: treat link status and placement from such a batch as unknown; verify placement by link transform with links loaded, or run the report with links loaded.
patterns.found_by: comparing the batch report with the same links loaded in one model
patterns.revit_versions: any

patterns.name: Dialog remembers another project's folder
patterns.meaning: A batch dialog pre-fills the output folder last used, which belonged to another project; accepted, this week's outputs land in the wrong project's report folder and the report reads stale data. Defence: type the output folder (project and date) on every run and check where files were written.
patterns.found_by: checking the output folder after the run
patterns.revit_versions: any; tool dialog

patterns.name: Panel schedule sheet read as empty
patterns.meaning: A rule that decides sheet content from viewports and ScheduleSheetInstance misses panel schedules: on a sheet they are PanelScheduleSheetInstance, a separate class. Panel-schedule-only sheets are reported as empty and drop out of print sets, transmittals or sheet checks. Defence: count PanelScheduleSheetInstance with the schedules, and compare the result with the model's sheet list once.
patterns.found_by: comparing a dry run with the electrical model's sheet list
patterns.revit_versions: 2024; class unchanged since panel schedules were introduced

patterns.name: Posted command waits on the Home screen
patterns.meaning: With no model open and Revit Home showing, a command started by UIApplication.PostCommand (here an add-in batch command) returns 'posted' but does not run; it runs only when Home is left. An agent that waits for a dialog sees nothing and may post again. Defence: leave Home (back arrow) or click the ribbon button, and take a screenshot after posting before anything else.
patterns.found_by: screenshots after posting the batch command

patterns.name: Closing the document the bridge holds
patterns.meaning: A bridge script passes one document as doc. Closing that document (for example in a loop over Application.Documents after opening the next model) throws InvalidObjectException, and the call reports an error although other documents in the loop did close. Defence: after OpenAndActivateDocument work on uiapp.ActiveUIDocument.Document, close only the previous model by the reference taken before opening, and close the active model with PostableCommand.Close; check the open documents after any error. Seen again 2026-10-28 with a background document: SynchronizeWithCentral followed by Close in the same call returned InvalidObjectException although sync and close had both happened; reopening confirmed the central model. Close in a separate call and check state after any error.
patterns.found_by: state check after the error

patterns.name: Schedule export repeats one element
patterns.meaning: An exported multi-category schedule can list one element on several rows (seen: multi-level stairs exported twice with the same element id). Counting rows reports duplicate keys that are not duplicates in the model. Defence: count and deduplicate export rows by unique id; check duplicates against the model before reporting them.
patterns.found_by: grouping the duplicate keys by element id

patterns.name: Placed spaces with no area because links are not room bounding
patterns.meaning: MEP spaces are placed but report area 0, so every instance's Space is empty and Space fields in schedules stay blank. The architectural link type in the MEP model has Room Bounding off. Defence: check space area before reading Space fields; set Room Bounding on the architecture and facade link types.
patterns.found_by: counting enclosed spaces and reading the link types

patterns.name: Electrical value read from the family instead of the circuit
patterns.meaning: Voltage on lighting fixtures, devices and equipment is usually empty or only a type value on the family; the real value is the circuit's. Mirroring the family parameter gives 0% fill. Defence: read voltage from the element's power circuit (ElectricalSystem); read load from the family's own load parameters or the sum of panel phase loads.
patterns.found_by: fill-rate check of the exported dataset

patterns.name: One field run as a list where the tool expects one value per run
patterns.meaning: A tool field that accepts a separated list (ZEN Type Marks by Family search strings) was filled with every group at once, while the tool's intended use is one group string per run, which also becomes the prefix. Defence: read the tool's summary after a trial run; run once per group.
patterns.found_by: owner review

patterns.name: A finished batch's completion dialog blocks the next call
patterns.meaning: The completion message of a batch run (ZEN ACC Gate 'Batch actions completed') stayed open after the run; the next bridge call waited 60 s and timed out. Defence: take a screenshot before the first bridge call after any batch run and close leftover dialogs.
patterns.found_by: screenshot after the timeout

patterns.name: A filter outside the reconciliation drops rows silently
patterns.meaning: A reader that keeps only rows with a given field (here: a unique id) drops every row without it before counting starts. The totals still reconcile because the dropped rows were never counted, so nothing looks wrong. Seen with nested parts in a BOM: they carry their parent's key but no id of their own. Defence: count every input row, and turn each row that is not used into a named exception, so 'read = used + exceptions' covers the whole input. Seen a second time the same day with system rows and sub-elements (stair runs, landings, supports, circuits) that have neither id nor key; fixed by reading every non-blank row.
patterns.found_by: comparing keys shared by rows with keys shared by unique elements
